tldr: Inverting the conventional motion-tracking baseline, this work first trains a general locomotion controller as the foundational substrate and integrates seven kicking skills via task gating. This achieves diverse strikes across a wide 259.5-degree nominal range and robust post-kick recovery without degrading locomotion performance.
hero_caption: Architecture comparison between prior work (left) and this approach (right). Prior methods make motion tracking the substrate and derive locomotion during ball approach. Here, a general locomotion policy is trained first as a shared hub (substrate), placing each kicking skill on top to reduce transitions to $O(N)$.
overview:
Humanoid soccer presents a challenging duality in whole-body control: free-form locomotion across the pitch, coupled with ball kicking where contact lasts less than 10 milliseconds. Prominent recent systems (such as RoboNaldo) use human motion tracking as their substrate, steering a motion-reference anchor toward the ball to derive locomotion. However, in this setup, locomotion is trained only during ball approaches. This sacrifices general mobility—such as lateral stepping, backward walking, and disturbance recovery—and binds kicks to a single motion clip.

To overcome this, the authors introduce a "Locomotion-Grounded" approach that flips the control stack upside down. First, in an environment without balls or motion clips, they train a robust locomotion policy capable of omnidirectional velocity tracking across rough terrain and disturbances. Using this solid locomotion policy as a shared composition hub (substrate), a skill library of seven human kicking motions is added using task gating (a mechanism where kick rewards and gradients are set to strict zero in locomotion mode).

The authors validated this approach in simulation and on real hardware using a 29-DoF full-sized humanoid, the Unitree G1. Adding the seven kicking skills caused at most a 0.04 MAE degradation in velocity tracking while covering a wide nominal aim direction of 259.5 degrees across the full library, including lateral, rearward, and weak-foot strikes. Furthermore, even from unstable post-impact states or aborted swings, the robot hands control back directly to the trained locomotion controller for stable walking recovery without relying on scripted poses.
contributions: Proposed a task-gated reinforcement learning architecture that uses a general locomotion policy as the substrate rather than motion tracking, hard-zeroing kick rewards during locomotion to prevent performance degradation.

Constructed a multi-directional kicking library of seven skills covering a nominal aim range of 259.5 degrees, incorporating lateral, rearward, and weak-foot strikes that a single forward-facing reference cannot express.
Eliminated scripted pose-recovery tails, introducing a direct handoff from high-momentum, single-support post-strike states back to the trained locomotion controller.
Quantitatively evaluated general locomotion performance—velocity tracking, rough terrain traversal, and push recovery—alongside shooting accuracy on hardware with the full skill library attached.

sections.heading: Flipping the Stack: Why Locomotion Comes First
sections.summary: Conventional humanoid soccer derived locomotion from motion tracking, leaving general mobility unevaluated and kicking variations narrow. This paper inverts the architecture by establishing a general locomotion policy as the base and layering kicking skills on top, achieving both versatile strikes and robust mobility.
sections.details:
Realizing agile locomotion and high-impact kicks within a single humanoid hardware and control framework is exceptionally difficult. Prior systems like RoboNaldo retarget human kicking motions and track them with rewards, steering that reference anchor toward the ball to achieve impressive shooting results.

However, this approach suffers from two overlooked shortcomings:

- Skewed and unevaluated locomotion: Locomotion is practiced only while approaching the ball. Omnidirectional commands like lateral shuffling, reversing, or in-place turning are never honed, and resilience to rough terrain or pushes remains untested.
- Confinement to a single motion: Relying on one reference clip prevents weak-foot strikes, sideways passes, or rearward clearances that dynamic match play requires.

To resolve this, the authors adopt Substrate Inversion. They first train a robust locomotion policy tracking omnidirectional velocity commands in an environment free of balls or motion clips. On top of this substrate, $N$ kicking skills are layered using task gating (reward and gradient terms for kicking are hard-zeroed during locomotion). As a result, all skills start from and return to this shared commandable state, achieving $O(N)$ transitions instead of $O(N^2)$. Furthermore, post-strike stabilization is handed back directly to the trained locomotion controller rather than handled by per-clip hand-authored scripts.

sections.heading: Prior Art and the Blind Spot of Independent Locomotion
sections.summary: While reinforcement learning for humanoid soccer and motion tracking has advanced rapidly, locomotion capabilities have rarely been evaluated independently from ball approach, and wide-angle aiming has not been framed as an explicit command. This work leverages the options framework and policy distillation to integrate skills around a locomotion hub.
sections.details:
### II-A Humanoid Soccer and Robot Sports
Robot soccer has progressed from 1-on-1 matches with small bipeds to direct whole-body striking on full-sized humanoids. Recent efforts such as SkillX combine vision-based kicking, trapping, dribbling, and shooting into a single policy. However, these systems still focus on a single kick toward a fixed goal or transition directly between skills without a shared locomotion state. While RoboNaldo achieved strong shooting performance, general locomotion and rearward striking were not evaluated.

### II-B Motion Tracking, Locomotion, and Manipulation Primitives
Motion tracking effectively coordinates whole-body actions, but it over-constrains contact timing and poses. In this work, task-mode gating addresses this by completely switching off tracking objectives outside the skill. Additionally, because ball impact is an impulse lasting under 10 milliseconds where rewards register only after departure, maintaining balance right after strike is critical.

### II-C Skill Libraries, Composition, and Transitions
Viewed through the lens of the options framework in reinforcement learning, having a shared hub ensures the termination set of one skill lies within the initiation set of the next. Instead of learning $O(N^2)$ pairwise transitions between skills, composition simplifies to $O(N)$ through the locomotion hub. Here, specialized expert policies are trained for each skill and then distilled via behavioral cloning into a single unified student network.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Task Gating and Explicit Aim Commands
sections.summary: To switch between locomotion and kicking within a single policy, the system employs hard task-mode gating. Aim targets are given as relative angles from each skill's nominal direction rather than world coordinates, enabling localization-free control.
sections.details:
### III-A Task-Mode Gating
The overall system is formulated as a single Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each environment holds a task-mode variable $m_t \in \{\text{loco}, \text{kick}\}$. Crucially, rewards outside the active mode are not merely discounted—they are hard-zeroed. Experiments revealed that leaving even a small tracking weight (e.g., 0.1x or 0.5x) monotonically degraded locomotion, increasing backward walking MAE by up to 0.33. Irrelevant observation segments (within the 261-dimensional observation vector) are zero-masked, and an explicit one-hot signal indicates the active mode.

### III-B Skill Conditioning
In kick mode, the retargeted reference trajectory is fed into the observation. Rather than specifying the goal as a fixed point in world coordinates, the target is defined relative to the ball position $p_{\text{ball}}$ and the skill's nominal striking direction $\beta$. A relative target angle $\theta \in [-\theta_{\text{max}}, \theta_{\text{max}}]$ (set to $\pm 15^\circ$) at a distance $D = 5$ m is normalized as a command $\theta_{\text{aim}} \in [-1, 1]$. This standardized command allows aim adjustment across all skills without relying on global localization.

### III-C Handoff to Locomotion
When the authored reference motion finishes, the mode automatically reverts to `loco`, and the trained locomotion policy assumes control. Rather than tracking a scripted pose-recovery trajectory, the robot hands the dynamic momentum and single-support state of the follow-through directly over to the disturbance-resilient locomotion controller.

sections.heading: Four-Stage Curriculum and the Distillation Pipeline
sections.summary: The training pipeline spans four stages: locomotion foundation, motion tracking, targeted striking, and multi-skill distillation into a single network. It incorporates balance-potential shaping to counter vanishing gradients near tipping points and trains recovery from live kick states.
sections.details:
Training is implemented via FastSAC (off-policy maximum entropy RL) in IsaacLab across the four stages illustrated in Fig. F2.

### IV-A & IV-B & IV-C Stages 1–3: From Foundation to Specialized Kickers
- Stage 1 (Locomotion Substrate): Trains a pure locomotion policy tracking omnidirectional velocity commands $(v_x, v_y, \omega_z)$ over rough terrain with mass and friction randomization, without balls or reference motions.
- Stage 2 (Motion Tracking): Introduces kick environments and adds human-retargeted tracking rewards. Kick rewards remain zero here to focus solely on whole-body coordination.
- Stage 3 (Targeted Striking): Kick rewards are ramped up while target angles $\theta$ vary by $\pm 15^\circ$ and initial ball positions vary by $\pm 10$ cm.

Key to this stage is "balance-potential shaping." Conventional Gaussian tracking rewards saturate near zero when a fall starts, losing gradient signals, while survival bonuses lack directional gradient entirely. By introducing a potential $\Phi = \Phi_{\text{bal}}\Phi_{\text{ht}}$ based on capture-point margins relative to the support polygon and center-of-mass height, the policy receives informative gradients even in near-fall states. Additionally, perturbed states from live kick environments are fed into the locomotion environment as initial conditions, training seamless handoffs from disrupted postures.

### IV-D Stage 4: Multi-Skill Distillation (DAgger)
Individual expert policies trained on each kicking skill are distilled into a single student policy $\pi_\theta$ using DAgger-style behavioral cloning. Querying expert actions on states visited by student rollouts ensures robust recovery even if the student drifts into unfamiliar states.

### IV-E & IV-F Algorithm and Domain Randomization
FastSAC provides high sample efficiency, using mode-dependent discount factors $\gamma(m_t)$ and entropy coefficients $\alpha(m_t)$. Extensive domain randomization covers internal joint friction, simulator contact-solver parameters, and ball observation latency and dropout to bridge the reality gap.

captions.F2: Training pipeline (left) and hardware deployment stack (right). Stages A through C progressively train kick experts from the locomotion base, and Stage 4 unifies them into a single network via DAgger distillation. On hardware, onboard LiDAR and camera track the ball, outputting 29-DoF joint position commands via the task-mode gate.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup: 29-DoF Humanoid and 7 Kicking Skills
sections.summary: Policies trained in IsaacLab on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 were evaluated in MuJoCo (sim-to-sim) and on physical hardware. The skill library consists of seven kicking skills covering forward, lateral, and rearward directions.
sections.details:
### V-A Robot Platform and Skill Library
Experiments were conducted on the 29-DoF full-sized humanoid Unitree G1. The policy runs at 50 Hz, outputting joint position targets. While training used IsaacLab in parallel, simulation benchmarks were exported to MuJoCo to evaluate across a sim-to-sim gap. On physical hardware, ball positions are tracked using a head-mounted MID-360 LiDAR and a 2-DoF pan-tilt ZED Mini camera.

The library consists of seven kicking skills shown in Table IV. Nominal aim angles include forward ($0^\circ$), right-leaning ($-28.2^\circ$), left instep ($+47.6^\circ$), left rearward ($+137.8^\circ$), and right rearward ($-121.7^\circ$), collectively spanning $259.5^\circ$.

### V-B Metrics and Protocols
Shooting performance is evaluated by success rates at 0.5 m (tolerance $\pm 5.7^\circ$) and 1.0 m radii targeting a 5 m distance, along with peak ball velocity and contact rate. Locomotion is measured by velocity tracking MAE, rough terrain traversal distance, and push-recovery success. To account for checkpoint variance, results report median values across checkpoint sweeps rather than a single run.

sections.heading: Results: Versatile Shooting Meets Uncompromised Locomotion
sections.summary: The consolidated policy covers a nominal aim range of 259.5 degrees, validating lateral and rearward strikes as well as walking-to-kick transitions on hardware. Locomotion tracking MAE degraded by at most 0.04 with the full skill library attached, and the system demonstrated robust recovery even from aborted kicks.
sections.details:
### VI-A Shooting Quality and Hardware Validation
The forward-kick expert (skill_1) achieved a 44.3% success rate within a 0.5 m radius at 5 m. In the 7-skill distilled policy, this dropped to 10.2% (15.4% library average), while preserving multi-directional capabilities. Peak ball speeds were moderate (2.0 to 4.1 m/s) compared to prior work (e.g., RoboNaldo's 13 m/s), representing a design trade-off prioritizing whole-body stability and broad aim coverage over maximum striking force. Physical hardware tests (Fig. F3) verified forward, lateral, and rearward strikes, as well as kicks initiated from commanded walking approaches.

### VI-B Skill Coverage and Distillation Interference
As shown in Fig. F4, the seven skills cover a wide area around the robot. Even when the initial ball position was placed outside the training envelope ($\pm 20$ cm), the contact rate remained at 70.4%. However, scaling the integrated library from $N=2$ to $N=7$ caused the average success rate to decline monotonically from 26.0% to 15.4%. Negative transfer during distillation proved to be a notable bottleneck, particularly for high-torsion rearward strikes (skill_2).

### VI-C Robustness of Locomotion Handoff
The policy achieved a 98.8% success rate in returning to stable locomotion post-kick. It also recovered reliably when a swing was aborted mid-motion (confirmed on hardware, Table IX (b)). In dynamic walking-to-kick transitions, higher approach velocities decreased accuracy (0.5 m success dropped from 17.0% to 11.9%), yet fall rates stayed low at 4.2%, surviving 95.8% of attempts.

### VI-D Locomotion Generality
As detailed in Table XI, holding the entire kicking library increased velocity-tracking MAE by at most 0.04 compared to a locomotion-only baseline—on par with baseline seed variance. Rough terrain traversal and push recovery remained virtually identical, demonstrating that acquiring kicks does not compromise base mobility.

sections.heading: Limitations and Conclusion: Distillation Losses and Calibration
sections.summary: This work demonstrates a new paradigm for humanoid soccer founded on general locomotion. While performance drops during multi-skill distillation and systematic angular offsets remain challenges, post-hoc calibration significantly recovers accuracy, validating the co-existence of broad mobility and diverse kicks.
sections.details:
### VII-A Limitations
The primary open challenge is that shooting success rates drop by roughly half when distilling specialized experts into a single unified policy (from 33.2% teacher average down to 15.4%).
Additionally, striking trajectories exhibit skill-specific systematic angular offsets (up to $\approx 40^\circ$) and trial-to-trial variance ($9^\circ \text{ to } 24^\circ$). However, fitting and compensating for these systematic biases from test rollouts (angle calibration) boosted success rates by a factor of 1.7 to 1.8 (Table XII).

### VII-B Conclusion
This study inverts the established convention of deriving locomotion from motion tracking, demonstrating an architecture where kicking skills are layered onto a locomotion substrate. Task gating preserves locomotion capabilities while uniting a 7-skill, 259.5-degree kicking library into a single network, fully validated on physical humanoid hardware.

takeaways: Making motion tracking the substrate restricts the locomotion distribution; establishing an omnidirectional, disturbance-resilient locomotion base first and gating skills on top preserves mobility.
When multi-tasking across distinct operational modes, setting inactive rewards to hard zero rather than soft discounts is vital to prevent performance degradation.
Using a shared locomotion state as a hub avoids brute-force $O(N^2)$ pairwise transitions, enabling $O(N)$ scalability when composing and adding skills.
Distilling multiple dynamic, impulse-driven contact tasks via DAgger induces noticeable negative transfer; post-hoc systematic bias correction is effective in recovering accuracy.
limitations: Shooting accuracy drops by more than half when distilling multi-skill experts into a single student policy due to representational capacity and task interference.
Strikes exhibit significant skill-specific systematic angular offsets (up to $40^\circ$), requiring per-checkpoint aim calibration.
Peak ball velocities are kept modest ($2 \text{ to } 4$ m/s) to ensure whole-body balance, falling short of high-speed strikes seen in prior single-motion work (13 m/s).
Shooting accuracy drops by roughly 30% when initiating kicks from higher walking approach velocities.
